s1.why: [2] lists the same five processes as possible parts of mountain building and [6] lists the same five main types; the joining word 'giving' is loose but adds no new fact.

s2.why: [16] says volcanic arcs form at oceanic-continental boundaries while folding occurs at continental-continental boundaries.

f0.why: [6] names the five main types: volcanic, fold, plateau, fault-block and dome.

q1.why: [12] says a shield volcano has a gently sloping cone because of low-viscosity basalt; [13] gives Mauna Loa as the example. The 'spreads far' gloss is extra but the answer does not depend on it.

q2.why: [15] says colliding plates buckle and fold, forming mountains; [16] places folding at continental-continental boundaries and arcs at oceanic-continental ones.

q3.why: [10] says most volcanoes occur in a band encircling the Pacific, with another from the Mediterranean across Asia.

q4.why: [21] says spreading causes tensional forces; [22] says when the plate splits a center block drops down relative to its flanking blocks.

q5.why: [9] says a volcanic arc forms near a subduction zone where the sinking oceanic crust melts and drags water down.

q6.why: [13] says stratovolcanoes have steeper cones from higher viscosity and more violent, less frequent eruptions than shields; [14] lists Mount Fuji as an example.

b0.why: [12] ties low-viscosity basalt to a gentle cone and [13] ties higher viscosity to the steeper 33-40 degree cone, with Mauna Loa at 4-6 degrees; answer a follows.

b1.why: [13] puts Mauna Loa and 4-6 degrees with shields, and 33-40 degrees plus more violent, less frequent eruptions with stratovolcanoes; [14] lists Fuji and Vesuvius as examples.

b2.why: [20] defines horsts as higher blocks and grabens as troughs; [9] puts volcanic arcs near subduction zones; [10] describes the Ring of Fire band around the Pacific.

b3.why: [21] and [22] give the first three steps, and [22] says the center block drops down, so the fourth step (index 3, 'rises') is the wrong one.
